title: EDGAR Next Webinar, Enrollment and FAQs – August 26, 2025 (Live Recording)
description:
The EDGAR Business Office hosted a live webinar regarding EDGAR Next enrollment and frequently asked questions about EDGAR Next on Tuesday, August 26 from 2:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
For additional information about EDGAR Next, please visit the EDGAR Next page on SEC.gov.
 
https://www.sec.gov/submit-filings/improving-edgar/edgar-next-improving-filer-access-account-management

Disclaimer: EBO staff in their official capacity facilitated the webinar, however, comments made during the webinar do not necessarily reflect the views of the Commission, the Commissioners, or other members of the staff.

*** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

I think you can find out on the web page. I'm sorry for that. You certainly can you take advantage also of the tips, complaints and referral system if that does help. Or you can call the Office of Investor Education and Advocacy. They also have a number they'll answer. Is there any others we can answer quickly? Guys, I know we're past time. I'm just trying to scroll through to see if there's any recurring issues that are there ones I see somebody mentioning again, the driver's license for login.gov. We don't need your driver's license number. We're not asking for any of that. You just need to have your e-mail select the multi factor authentication method and you should be able to obtain your login.gov credentials. You should not be applying. Try to go to login. gov through the Edgar link. That should bring you to the correct authentication level. Perhaps people are going there without using that link. Oh, you know one thing I want to mention. There's a question here. So that's we have to watch out for. So that's, that's the worst case scenario. So please, if you share the client with someone else, please talk to the client, confirm that you know who the other parties are, and then agree on a date when enrollment will occur and make sure everyone's notified. So if you've rushed ahead and enrolled with a client early, the other people are not going to know and they're going to get upset because as part of the enrollment process I do, the CCC does get reset. If you go in there, you should be able to manage your emails. So reason to enroll historical filers that is because we need to move all of our filers over. If you're going to continue to file, you'll need to log in with these individual credentials and you'll need to have a dashboard where people are authorized and where there's a confirmation annually. But, and I'm not sure that what what you're meaning there, but that's, that's the option, yeah. So if it takes more than ten days, what should I do? Like an exemption, You know, you're not going to get an exemption. I mean, you need to go ahead. Thank you all for joining us today. I hope that we were able to answer at least some of your questions. title: 2025 09 29 SEC CFTC Roundtable Meeting Part 03
description:
*** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

Follow the SEC:
Twitter: https://twitter.com/SECGov
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/SECGov
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/us-securities-and-exchange-commission
transcript: All right, so why don't we go ahead and kick off our third and final panel hear from the participants. So as Co-moderators, again, the theme of the day is SEC, CFTC collaboration. We're rejoined by former CFTC chair Chris Giancarlo and we're joined by former SEC chair and founder of Parades Strategies, Troy Paredes. So gentlemen, take it away. All right, thanks, everybody. Looking forward to another lively discussion here. So Chris and I have the great pleasure to moderate, Co-moderate today's panel #3 which is focused on how regulatory harmonization could increase choice for market participants and reduce costs for investors, building on a lot of what has been covered on the 1st 2 panels. So what I'm going to do just to kick us off, I'm just going to do a two second intro of, of each person, very distinguished backgrounds, but I'll just give a quick name, title, affiliation so we can all Orient ourselves. And then I'll hand it to to Chris and we'll, we'll go from there. So today we have, and I think I got the order right. We have Steven Berger from Citadel, Managing Director of Government and Regulatory Policy. And apologies if I get any names mispronounced here. I know I got your name, your name right. We got Ryan Levar from Wisdom Free, Chief Local Officer and Head of Business and Legal Affairs, Digital Assets, Nick Lundgren from crypto.com, Chief Legal Officer, JB, JB McKenzie from Robin Hood Markets, Vice President, General Manager, Futures and International, Dave Olsen, Jump Trading Group President and Chief Investment Officer, Sonali Theisen, global head of FIC electronic trading and market strategic investments at Bank of America, and Brad Tolley, JP Morgan, Managing Director and global head of corporate derivatives and private side sales and head of America sales. I hope I got all of that correct. Anybody can correct the record if I got anything I got anything wrong. So before I hand it to Chris, let me just make one quick just perspective thought from my perspective. One of the things so interesting about this particular day and the round table is there was reference to the last time there was a round table like like this between the SEC and the CFTC and it was around Title 7 of Dodd Frank. And I happened to be at the SEC at the time and recall just one, the rarity of those things occurring and #2 the, the, the benefits and, and sure, we can talk about the big picture benefits and all other kinds of way to try ways to try to facilitate harmonization, but sometimes just getting folks together can actually serve a real beneficial impact. So I very much commend Chairman Atkins and Acting Chair Pham for their leadership in terms of today. And I know from what they've said publicly, their prioritization of, of the, of the efforts towards, towards harmonization. The the other quick thing I would note, which is in a more on a substantive, substantive front. One of the things that I, I find just so fascinating about the whole discussion around harmonization and the, the two agencies is, and I'm going to way oversimplify here, but just for the sake of, for the sake of brevity, one way to think about their respective jurisdictions and, and markets and the like is from the perspective of the underlying authorizing statutes, rules, regulations. And I won't go through the list, but if you take a list of all the different kind of acronyms for SEC market participants and then compare all the, you know, list of acronyms for CFTC market participants, that that is a way you're thinking about it in terms of regulated status, for example, under whether it's the federal securities laws on the one hand or the Commodity Exchange Act on the other. That is a way of approaching things. Another way of approaching things is to focus and again, at the risk of oversimplification on the economics, on the markets, on the risks and the exposures and what it is that market participants are looking to achieve or what it is they're looking to avoid. Now, one would hope that all that eventually lines itself up, but those are two different, different takes. And, and so to, to, to that kind of recognition from my perspective, thinking about harmonization and how it maps to, to those considerations, I just find to be a fascinating topic. So with those preliminaries out of the way, Chris, why don't I hand it to you? Actually, Troy, I'm going to actually pick up on on that concept you introduced with an anecdote as a way of introducing our first discussion point. Before I went into serving in government, I was one of the principles in a a firm that was an inter dealer broker on Wall Street that was a firm that helped major financial institutions trade between each other. You might say we were in exchange for things that didn't trade on a regulated exchange. And in our case, one of our largest product areas was in the area credit default swaps. About 2/3 of the credit default swap market traded through our platforms here in the United States and around the world prior to Dodd Frank and prior to the financial crisis. All of those swaps traded on in, in, in cohesive liquidity pools. They were not separated out. There was no separation between broad based swaps and single name credit default swaps. They traded together. There might be a Latin American desk or North American desk, but they traded in one liquidity pool. Well, along comes Dodd Frank and Dodd Frank suddenly announced that our business which antecedents went back over 100 years was a swap execution facility. A nice made-up name somewhat describe what we did, but anyway, that was our regulatory classification. But more importantly, it divided swaps up into narrow base swaps and broad based swaps subject to separate regulatory schemes and subject to different self regulation. Some of our brokers now we're NFA regulated, registered somewhere, FINRA registered. And what we had to do was separate those liquidity pools into separate desks. So of course, it seemed like a good idea at the time to Congress as the Reg committee and the Banking Committee are trying to reach a compromise. But it had real world effects, not just on our platform, but more importantly the market participants that trade in our platform suddenly didn't get the benefit of a cohesive liquidity pool, but liquidity pools, to your point, Trey, that were divided into separate areas. So I think it was Terry Duffy on the last panel who said that what we always need to do is focus on the patients. Well, today we have the patients. This panel is the patients. This is a panel of market participants and it's like the last panel, it's diverse. Some of the market participants on this panel are really concerned with wholesale trading as my former firm was. Others are really focused on the retail side. And so it's really an opportunity now to dig into what ultimately we're all here to focus on is how to market participants participate in these regulated markets and how do they navigate the differences between the rulemaking of the CFTC and the SEC. And hopefully maybe we can find in our conversation this afternoon ways in which those differences are not so distinct as the separate liquidity pools into separate into separate silos. So with that, I'd like to kick off and just talk about if we could and maybe maybe we'll start with Steven down the other end of the table and work away this way. What are some of the issues that the lack of coordination or simply the, the regulatory structure inherited by Congress, by the agencies impose on the markets and the, and the ultimately the clients that you serve? Thank you. And and look, I'd, I'd like to start by just first thanking Chairman Atkins, acting Chairman Pham and the SEC and CFTC commissioners and staff for organizing this afternoon's landmark discussion. And, and thank you to Chris and Troy for, for moderating and for your past invaluable service at both agencies. I applaud the SEC and CFTC harmonization effort to quote reduce unnecessary barriers, enhance market efficiency and createspace for innovation to thrive. And I concur that we have a generational opportunity here to further strengthen the preeminent position of US capital markets for both investors and issuers and to pave the way for future market evolution, integrating new technologies into our markets and unleashing innovation with respect to new products, innovations and trading, clearing settlement transparency and collateral mobility. And we can achieve this without either the SEC or CFTC losing sight of of their core missions. And, and I think we all acknowledge that in furtherance of those missions, the agencies still have a valuable role to play in overseeing both existing and nascent markets. Now look, I think it's clear from the historical context we, we heard earlier why, you know, there are separate SEC and CFTC regulatory regimes for the securities markets and for the futures and swaps markets respectively. But it's clear also that as these markets have grown and become more integrated and as market participants have innovative and diversified to better serve issuers, investors and hedgers, we've all witnessed how duplicative, inconsistent or contradictory frameworks have hindered growth, innovation and competitiveness and and acted as a de facto tax both on issuers and investors. So you know to your question Chris, you know for example, investment funds are are subject to overlapping registration, record keeping, reporting and exam requirements. I think Commissioner Uyeda did did a good job of highlighting some of those just now. Intermediaries are duly registered as broker dealers in FCMS and in some cases as both swap dealers and security base swap dealers, which comes with their own slew of overlapping and often contradictory regulatory requirements. Providers of clearing services have to navigate multiple regimes, DCOs on the CFTC side and clearing agencies on the SEC side. You know, I think it's wonderful news that we have ICE and CME entering the market to provide clearing services for U.S. Treasuries. For example, having, you know, the two strongest futures exchanges in the United States coming into that market is a great development. But it pains me to hear that, you know, there was a six effort, a six year effort. That was a false start in that front and that was a squandered opportunity. And and then Chris, as you just noted, we have a logical splits in the rules and oversight of markets that are otherwise economically unified, unified. So swaps versus security based swaps most notably in the credit space is an excellent example of that. Cash Treasuries versus Treasury futures is another I think notable example. And and I guess I would also like to point out that we shouldn't lose sight of the fact that the regulatory inefficiency extends down to the SRO level as well. So some of the issues we have probably with respect to SEC and CFTC harmonization, I would argue maybe even more pronounced for those of us who deal with both FINRA and NFA oversight, where we also have duplication, inconsistency and contradictions that are arguably even worse. So just a few like 3-3 areas I think I would highlight for where I think there's opportunities for meaningful progress. Look, the US asset management sector across both traditional and alternative investment funds is an unparalleled American asset, optimizing the allocation of capital to our economy and delivering returns for investors saving for their children's education or for their own retirement. To deliver on that, asset managers rely on the ability to invest in hedge across equities, options, futures, bonds and swap markets. So they're investing in asset classes that fall under both the SEC and the CFTCs jurisdiction. But unfortunately, as I just noted, that's left them a subject to two sets of registration, record keeping, reporting and exam requirements. And in the past we've dealt with that by appropriately tailored exemptions to let them fall under the appropriate regime. There's been already today good discussion with respect to portfolio margining and cross margining where we have opportunities to improve capital efficiency and pricing efficiency across correlated assets. At the same time, historical attempts so far to bridge the bifurcated regimes have yielded at times imperfect compromises that have impaired the predictability and durability of cross margin agreements, which is highly problematic in in times of stress and and can be pro cyclical. So we should expand opportunities for portfolio and cross margining, but also make sure that they're durable and resilient, including in times of stress. And then lastly, I think there's further opportunities to enhance the comprehensive and timely post trade transparency that's generally a hallmark of America's capital markets. It's clearly the norm in the equities, options, corporate bond, municipal bond and swaps markets. I think there's an interesting divergent with respect to our Treasury markets where treasury futures are subject to a timely and comprehensive post trade transparency framework. Cash treasuries still are not. And at best we have end of the day public reporting for the on the road segment of the market only. That's, that's Steven. Terrific remarks. Can I just ask you to put a pin in the issue of the different self regulatory organizations because we're having a great conversation today about harmonization of the two agencies. And yet do we need to have another conversation about greater harmonization between NFA and and FINRA and, and what are the areas where a firm like yours that's so comprehensively regulated faces challenges with the different self regulatory structures that those two enterprise, those two firm, those two agencies, sorry, organizations I present. Could you just come comment on that briefly go to Ryan. Yeah, sure. I mean, I think it manifests itself as, as as I alluded to both with respect to investment advisors and investment funds who will end up having to deal with both FINRA and NFA and with, you know, again with respect to registration, record keeping and exams. And then it manifests itself on for duly registered BDF, CMS as well. So it's, you know, I, I think there's already a healthy discussion about the amount of the functions that have been handed down to the SRO's from the agencies themselves. But I think to your point, there's even less perhaps coordination that occurs at that level. And we're, we're also sort of in the process of potentially putting even additional products and asset classes under the jurisdiction of these SRO's moving forward. So I think we should be cognizant of, of, of that lack of harmonization as well. And in my in my question, I didn't mean to in any way indicate that they're not forward leaning on this. Certainly in my experience working with NFA, they've always been very far leaning. But I think this new initiative toward greater corporation is going to present some, some, some workload for them that that perhaps it hasn't been in their wheelhouse so far. Ryan, do you want to comment on some areas in which the the degree of harmonization or lack of harmonization has been challenging for for you and your customer base much more retail oriented. Yeah, yeah. So see how, you know, it's funny because I was really going to focus on my example of 4.5, which chair you to certainly spend some time on before the break. And you know, but, but echoing that, you know, is, is a registered fund provider, you know, that, that then has funds that invest in commodity interests. And then having that CFTC overlap at the time, it really did create 2 bifurcated regulatory regimes that needed to be complied with. So, you know, personnel costs and the like. But but Commissioner Uyeda, really spending good time, I think, talking through those issues. So I'll maybe pivot to kind of another topic. I think more recently is really just the jurisdictional divide between the SEC and the CFTC on digital asset classification. So as we think about that, it comes up in a couple different contexts where, you know, if we're trying to launch an exchange traded product that's holding a digital asset, we have to ask ourselves, are we going to end up, you know, as a SEC registered 1940 act fund which typically invests in securities or might it be a 33 act only registered product which is holding typically commodities. And so even to this day, we're still looking at assets, trying to do an analysis to really understand what bucket does that fit in? You know, under the prior regime, it was or the SEC looking at really those assets and saying nearly every type of asset in this category would be a security. So that made it even more challenging if there were starting to get more, more clarity there, But but that's a challenge. And then we switched to or, or also we're, we're focused on really tokenized assets, so not digital assets themselves that are sort of native crypto to say a blockchain like Bitcoin or, or ether, but instead tokenizing real world assets, whether those are funds or commodities or the like. And so even a particular in the prior administration, you know, there could be some challenges there. And really is that tokenized assets that might generally look like a commodity? Is it in fact or or not in fact, but is the is, is the view being taken that that's in fact a, a security? And so, so that was challenging really trying to, you know, really navigate, you know, those two different regulatory regimes to try to land, you know, in the right regulated products structure. So I think looking at the history, that's certainly been a challenge. I know spend a little bit more time moving forward here in a second, but I'll stop there. Hey, Ryan, just to stick with you for a minute and then Nick, we'll we'll come to you. How does this manifest itself in terms of the impacts? Yeah, Well, it's a great question because well, I think one of the challenges is just take it from the FCCs perspective going back a year and and more in terms of characterizing, you know, you're dealing with a 1940s court case, Howie, you're then dealing with a a multi 30 plus prong sort of investment contract framework. You layer on another case called Gary plastic it, you know, you could, you could really trying to look at, you know, 30 to 40 factors to say is this asset not a security? And so it was really hard. Then you really want to stay on the right side of that asset character characterization. It's, it's a commodity, but you're, you know, spending time and energy on legal counsel, I mean, approaching for maybe one asset, you know. 6 figure legal analysis memorandum that ultimately you can either go to the staff with or or for your file and that takes time, energy staff to, you know, really all you're trying to do is make sure you're on the right side, in the right bucket. Nick, your firm is in a different business than than Wisdom Tree. What's what's your perspective? Well, First off, it's definitely a privilege to be here. If there's no contract, if there's no investment of money in a common enterprise, it cannot be a security. Since then, I think we've seen the CFTC not just take over what was predominantly A derivatives market, but start to exercise their spot market influence that's in place to prevent manipulation from occurring. First off, I want to thank again to Chair Pham and and Chair Atkins for having us here as Robin Hood. So I think for us as we look here, let's really think about how do we want to improve that experience and experience is going to improve it for every single person in this room. *** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

In practice it was a jurisdictional land grab. Mutual funds have long used derivatives as part of ordinary portfolio management, particularly for fixed income, where derivatives can often trade more easily and cheaply than the underlying securities. It meant duplicative reporting. Advisors had to build parallel systems to track, reconcile and report essentially the same information in two slightly different formats to two different regulators. Finally, it meant conflicting requirements. The SEC and CFTC had different standards for record keeping, advertising, and the use of third party administrators, funds that found themselves caught between two sets of rules that were not harmonized, and all of this translated into real cost. Industry feedback at the time foresaw millions of dollars in incremental compliance expenses, costs that were ultimately borne by investors. Yet there is no evidence that the CFT CS overlay produced any any incremental benefit in terms of market integrity or investor protection. So as technology continues to evolve in the financial sector, how can we avoid repeating this mistake? The CFTC and the SEC share responsibility for markets that are increasingly interwoven. The agencies need to look past technical definitions and focus on the functional aspects of the novel products themselves. What risks do they create? What practicalities already operate to mitigate those risks? How our remaining risks best address and how can duplication of effort be avoided? Today's call for harmonization and a new era of collaboration from the leaders of both agencies importantly make the point that we should answer these questions before announcing jurisdictional claims. We must remember alternatives to the alternative tools available to us, information sharing agreements, joint examinations, and harmonize reporting forms that help us work towards accountability without imposing duplicate requirements. The benefits of a successful regulatory engagement are clear, consistent rules, efficient compliance, and investor confidence. The consequences of failure are equally clear, duplicative oversight, higher costs and no discernible improvement in investor protection or market integrity. The pace of innovation in our markets is not slowing, it's quite the opposite. Today, this administration, we have an opportunity to avoid the mistakes of the past and instead together build a regulatory architecture that evolves with our markets and new financial products, not against them through a harmonized regulatory approach. They trade differently. They have similar, if not even greater levels of complexity and options. Anybody else want to weigh in on options before we move to Peter to talk about Canada and we'll talk about other markets. All right, so, so Peter, you want to talk about Canada, I think it's, you know, it's a really important thing for us to discuss. What about other markets that either have different trade through protections or no trade through protections at all? Because we don't we, we can't directly look at a counterfactual history. What if we had not put the order protection rule in? But what we can do is look at other markets and get experience from them that have either slightly different rules or no rules at all. So Peter, why don't you start us off here? And I know a lot of folks want to weigh in on this one. Yeah, just a quick history. In Canada, we don't have a SIP as I mentioned earlier. So when we had one marketplace back in 2006, the TMX, they were charging data fees to the street of a certain amount. And each new market when when competitive markets were were on boarded was able to charge data from day one. We were forced to connect to them because we had the notion of a trade through rule. So we were forced to connect to those marketplaces early on right away and they wrote the charge for market data. So what we were finding in Canada was a proliferation of markets that took place from the period of 2007 through to 2012. These markets weren't or non differentiated and were able to charge for market data. And as was talked about earlier, the connectivity costs upfront were very material to the brokerage community. So at in the around 2012, the regulators began to look at putting rules in place that would eliminate or at least create some sort of threshold required for for marketplaces to have orders protected. And in 2016, they introduced a rule that said and was originally proposed at 5%, but was lower to 2 1/2 than any market that had a not that had some form of a speed bump or a delay or had less than 2. 5% market share. That was no longer protected. That happened to be coincident with the last new marketplace we saw launched until one that's going to be launched later this year. So it literally has been 10 years. I don't want people to think that the reason there have been no new markets is because of that rule. I would argue it was more coincidental than anything else. And as I mentioned earlier, it was more driven by the by the industry's need to stop the parabolic increase in real time market data fees because these new marketplaces had no rules with respect to how they charge for data from day one. So in coincidence with the threshold rule, the regulators also created a rule that said your market share or the percentage of fees associated with real time market data needed to be somewhat linked to your market share. And that allowed the market to at least slow down the prolifer the increase in market data cost. So arguably to the to the point, we've heard earlier about whether or not a threshold will rule would lower costs on an ongoing basis. I don't think anyone disconnected from any of the venues that were less than 2 1/2%. Once you've dealt with those upfront costs plus the combination of of best tax requirements, essentially you've onboarded it and and absorb most of the cost. So I don't anticipate that you would see a significant number of of people disconnecting to those additional marketplace, especially if they're affiliated with exchanges you're already connected to. Quite possibly that reduces costs with respect to gateways and the like. The brand new marketplaces are the ones that require the significant upfront costs like 24. If you want to connect to them, you're going to need to create your own pay for all the associated costs of connecting. So again, I think the message there is that the threshold rule, yes, it did slow down or eliminate the proliferation of marketplaces in Canada, which I know is a goal a lot of people have with respect to 611. But it was again, more due to market data issues that the US doesn't face directly that we were facing in Canada. Anybody else want to weigh in on on Canada and for other venues? Yeah, I think it's instructive, but probably, you know, not to be lifted from Canada to the USI mean can't. All due respect to Peter, as you know, as he said, Canada is much smaller. We obviously operate many venues in Canada throughout acquisitions over the last few years. It's also important to note, I mean that the trade at effective trade at rule there is quite a bit different market structure than in the US. We can discuss whether or not a threshold makes sense, but we have not seen, even though we have one venue because of a delay that's not protected there. We have not seen disconnects dramatically because of that. So that's been our lived experience as well. Yeah, I'm not not suggesting the in terms of the trade out rule, if you look at dark trading in Canada, it's only 5 or 10% of the market. So I know there's been a lot of comments here about the proliferation of dark trading. Certainly the trade out rule that exists in Canada is the primary reason why we have a very low percentage of trade that happens in the dark or off exchange. That is absolutely the case. Whether that's good or bad you can debate, but that is definitely true. That's a sign. I guess maybe we'll have the mic. I'll mention obviously we operate the largest pan European exchange, both the UK and Europe and where we have a broad range of competitive, competitive leeway there. So we compete for a whole bunch of different trading mechanisms on exchange, off exchange, exchange trade reporting, a list of off exchange services there. There is obviously no rule 611, there is no order protection and BestX, there's BestX policies there. Some would say more stringent, some would say less than here. The market has figured it out there and so have we as a competitive exchange. So we, we could live without OPR. But I, we, as I said my opening statement, I don't think that get rid of getting rid of it without looking at everything else given the US size and structures is wise. But in Europe, we've seen quite a, quite a bit of growth given the ability for us to compete across the full spectrum of trading mechanisms. Thanks, Joe. Citadel obviously operates in a number of different markets. What sort of insights can we glean? Yeah, we're, we're, I, I I would just make 2 observations. 1, we are quite active in Europe, including on, on Chris's venue. And I would just be cautious about drawing too many conclusions about the US versus Europe. You look at the amount of volume, retail participation, the cost structure in Europe and there's clearly, you know some good companies and some good markets, but it pales in comparison to what we have in the US. And again, back to my earlier points, figuring out the contributing factors in the positives and negatives of some of the rules that we have in place here are very difficult. But I think pointing to one other market that has figured things out which we agree with, but then saying that's evidence that we should make the US market look more like that to me is a problematic thought process. The other thing I would say is we didn't talk about this directly, but just back to the opening presentation. I would also be very cautious about drawing conclusions about pre post trading and regular day trading when 611 is in place versus pre post when it's not. Because I would argue that at least for us, but I think for a lot of participants, everyone operates as if 611 was in effect during those periods of time. And so I would just say if you don't see in sentences of trade the role of trade throughs in those sessions, I don't think it's accidental. I think it's somewhat intentional. So I would, I would just keep that as a as a backdrop. Chris Slogan Yeah, so having an equity exchange that is small and could be impacted by any potential volume thresholds. We we kind of did some research and have some thoughts on this, right. So, you know, what do you calculate, right. Do you just look at only on exchange market share versus total market share including the TRF? Should we also exclude opening and closing auctions from volume which is not protected today and can skew cap calculations? So it doesn't seem fair to hold an exchange liable for volume and markets in which they can't compete such as over the counter or in or in the auction space. Also, a non protected exchange may have more volume in certain names in a protected venue and how do you reconcile not protecting one over the other in that name? So importantly, the trading volume threshold could be viewed as arbitrary. And then looking at like data on my ex Pearl, if our volume actually doubles when you exclude TRF data, we could also be higher if you exclude opening and closing auctions that are not protected and actually in tape B at times we could be over 4%. There's also volume and select symbols and tapes that exceeds exchanges with overall higher trading volumes. So why should those exchanges be protected when they have lower volume and select names or at or providing or execution quality in depth in those names when we than we are. So we would find that hard to reconcile it. We would challenge that, you know, anyone to reconcile a trading threshold with some of those aspects. Katie, did you want to weigh in here? I, I mean, I, I think what I just reiterate for both Canada and Europe and all the other regions in general is that yes, the markets are extremely different. I wouldn't just say very different. I would say the US markets extremely different from everything from the quality of the listed companies that are out there to trade to the volumes to the diversity of market participants. I would also concur from what I hear from my members with Peter that no one disconnected in Canada just because they were below that volume threshold. And then in Europe they do use a best ex regime. They actually from a more of a put more of a regulatory spend on it for Dave. They actually are looking at what we all look at on a customer perspective, let's call it the it's price that's quoted plus the external cost. So these are the venue fees, clearing and settlement fees. Everyone knows Europe has a lot more CSD's than we do over here with our one. So those costs are higher over there. Speed of execution, likelihood of percent of order getting executed, size, nature, etcetera. They are reviewed on those by their national regulators. But I would point out that a few years ago, both the UK and the EU got rid of the formal published reviews of those best acts because they just found that they were not used by investors and they were very costly and difficult to produce in there. Just the cost benefit analysis was not there. So I know Peter wants to weigh in again. And then Ari, you want to say a few words? Just a quick comment that we heard from my ex. I caution the Commission, if we are, we're looking at a threshold rule to avoid the complexity arguments that we just heard. If we get into individual stock market shares, it's just going to blow everything up in terms of complexity here. So I do think we have to be very, very careful. The threshold rule is at the marketplace level in Canada. And I'm not saying Canada by any means. Should Canada necessarily be a guidepost for how you would structure a threshold rule in the US? But the flip side of that is if we get down to looking at market shares on individual stocks or trying to take away certain parts of the market from that calculation, I think it'll be a rabbit hole you don't want to go down. Yeah, just quickly, we weren't advocating a per share or a symbol range threshold calculation. We were just trying to show that what some of the issues could be in trying to set a threshold to be protected or not. Thanks, Ari. Yeah, I guess just to reiterate what some of the other panel has said, I mean, you know, if and when hopefully we have a protected quote. I mean, is it 2.1%? Is it the overall Market Volume? How do you define it? You know, the devil's in the details, bottom line, but you know, hopefully allowing for innovation and innovate, the next intelligent cross to come, at least having an incubator to, to get up to that 1%, half percent, 2% threshold would be great. So it's going to, it's going to need a lot of thought. The only other thing I'd say is before we run out of time, I feel like maybe I need to click clarify my support for Dave Lauer given the rest of the the panel on BestX. But you know, now I feel like hesitant. So like, you know, I'm used to it. But yeah, but just just to clarify on BestX, one last point, you know, look again, we've gotten to where we are as a venue because people are do it not just looking at price, they're looking at other factors in going to intelligent cross. What I was, I guess trying to say back at the beginning of this panel is people are just not taking in our quote and we hear that is because of either we're not protected. So if people want to take in our quote, great, we'll sign everybody off tomorrow and then they can decide whether to act on that or not. But the point is we're just not seeing people take in the quote and we've heard part of it as BestX. Yeah, Dave, and then Joey, myself, Dave from supporting me. You know, I think that one thing to consider as well in Canada is that Canada is a good example of a market in which listings saw innovation and saw a disruption. And that has not happened in the US for quite some time. And any consideration of something like a market share threshold, I don't know if there's a great way to do it. But if if you do something like that and you don't consider potential innovation in listings, you've pretty much entrenched the listings duopoly here in the US. And you know that that is an area where there is, and I'm an advisor of the Green Impact Exchange, that's a new exchange that is about to launch and they're innovating in listings. And I think that that is something that we should want to see. As I talked about earlier here, we've seen fragmentation without innovation and it's all have been it's all been about copycat exchanges and latency rather than innovation and listings where one exchange did try to do it. And you know, I think that's something that we should encourage. And so we should be looking for ways to encourage innovation in parts of the market that haven't seen it and be more thoughtful about how we make exchange approvals before we continuously approve copycat exchanges. Joe, just one quick clarification and agreeing with with Ari on on part of his point. So we may not agree on the style of of quote that needs to get protected, but I wanted to be clear that our suggestion on a minimum market share threshold was for economic benefits, not for protected quote benefits. So we do think that having a threshold that introduces whether you have a protected quote or not can be potentially confusing to the marketplace and and difficult to administer. That was why we were intentionally suggesting that the market share threshold could be used to control the economic incentive to conduct a another medallion versus whether you have a protected quote or not. Chris, do you want to weigh in here, Chris? Oh, no, not right now. Thank you. We're almost done. So I'm going to ask folks. So if you have one, one last word, go ahead. Sure. Yeah, I just, I mean, a lot of the focus has been on exchange proliferation and copycat exchanges. And it's it's not that exchanges don't want to innovate, we do, but we are subject to Exchange Act standards when we file rule filings to adopt new technology or new functionality that has to go through a Commission review process. And no, not, not directly commenting on Jamie and his staff, but past staff have made it difficult for exchanges to push through things that are different. Everything has to be apples to apples. And the easiest way to market is to copy someone that's already doing it that the SEC has already approved. So it's not that we don't want to innovate. We are just a little hamstrung in innovating as compared to the over the counter market, which is able to innovate in a much more free form than exchanges are. And we would welcome the opportunity to innovate and to add more functionality to our markets should the SEC allow. Thank you. And for Chris, it's a brand new day at the SEC. Your mouth that God's ears a renaissance. So so we're going to close in just a minute here. Ask ask the panelists if there's anything that we did not get out on the table. Joe, I'll just say very quickly, I think this sort of came out, but it might be worth just spelling out. I think the one thing that came through very clearly in everyone's comments, whether explicit or not, is just the myriad of rules that have some tie in with 611, right? You've got the octopus, the octopus. And just to be we need to as an industry and as as the SEC, be thoughtful about how all of those fit together. And if we change 611, all the other rules that are going to have to be dressed alongside. Yeah, Yeah. I mean, in your closing remarks, I'd ask each of you to throw those out there. The 1st is if we're trying to reduce cost in with exchange connectivity and market data, the answer is a cost plus model, which is something that IDX has been advocating for and where they have in their filings, they're explicit delineated costs. And then the margins that they're putting on top of that, something that Europe has tried to move to with, you know, somewhat not as much success, something that I've also been pushing for in Canada as Canada revisits its market data cost regime. So you know, I think that would do the most to reduce cost and complexity, not necessarily much complexity, but at least cost. *** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

transcript: Welcome back to the afternoon session of our September 18th, 2025 Investor Advisory Committee meeting. Andrew, do we need to note if any IAC members have joined or departed as we're returning to the public session? Yes, thank you, Brian. So Sergio Rodrigo is still online as well as Christine Lazaro. It does not look like Alvin Velasquez is online. And I will note that Gina-Gail joined us in person during the morning session. Thank you so much, Andrew. Our afternoon session begins with Part 2 of our panel reconsidering the eligibility criteria and regulatory treatment of foreign private issuers. It's moderated by George Georgiev followed by a discussion of potential committee recommendations later this afternoon beginning at approximately 330. George. Thank you, Brian and welcome back everyone. So we're going to proceed with Part 2 of our discussion on the regulatory treatment of foreign private insurance, following on in part on the SEC's concept release on the same topic from June of this year. We got a lot of very helpful information this morning and we have two distinguished panelists with us today for a more technical discussion about the some of the specific problems with the current FBI regime and then some of the solutions that may be available to the Commission. We have Jeff Mahoney, who is the General Counsel of the Council of Institutional Investors, representing the institutional investor perspective. Thank you for being here, Jeff. And we also have Paul Dudek, who is no stranger to the building. He used to be the Chief of the SEC's Office of International Corporate Finance and very well known to capital markets lawyers working in this space. He is currently a partner at Latham and Watkins. And he also is one of the primary drafters of a comment letter that addressed some of these issues in the potential solutions. And I should also mention, of course, that Jeff wrote the comment letter on behalf of CII and also was involved in a very helpful report on the VIE structure. So a lot of knowledge on the panel. And without further ado, I will turn it over to Jeff to get us started. Good afternoon. I want to thank you for Professor Georgiev, Investor Advisory Committee Chair, Brian Shorr, other members of the committee for the opportunity to speak with you again today. I'm appearing here today on behalf of the Council of Institutional Investors, CI as a nonprofit, a non partisan association with a core membership that includes US asset owners with assets under management of approximately $5 trillion. Those member funds to major long term share owners with the duty to protect the retirement savings of millions of workers and their families, including public pension funds with more than 15,000,000 participants. These are true and real Main St. investors through their pension funds. Our associate members include non-us asset owners, approximately 5 trillion in assets under management, and a range of asset managers with more than 74 trillion in assets under management. As Commissioner Hester Peirce noted in her June 4th statement in response to the concept release, she said that one of the animating principles of the Commission's past rulemakings related to foreign private issuer eligibility has been the notion that various accommodations and relief from domestic rules are appropriate because foreign companies are subject to meaningful regulation and disclosure obligations in their home jurisdiction. I think many would agree that that principle is fundamentally sound. And 20 years ago, when the SEC last addressed foreign private issuers, that principle fit neatly with the composition of 20F filers that at the time were predominantly incorporated and headquartered in Canada and the United Kingdom. But you Fast forward to the present day and it appears that the principle that govern the SEC is thinking about foreign private issuers 20 years ago is now routinely contravene by many of today's foreign companies. More specifically, the Cayman Islands in China are now the preferred location of incorporation and headquarters, respectively, for foreign private issuers. Although China is developing a securities regulatory regime, I think few would argue that it provides meaningful investor protections when compared quickly when compared to the United States and many experts view China as possessing an immature disclosure system. That leaves investors and I'll just as described in this temporary better markets comment letter, It leaves investors with quote, a severe asymmetry information problem. And as NASDAQ recently observed in connection with a proposed change to their listing standards, they said the unique risks that Chinese companies present the US investors due to barriers on access to information and limitations on the ability of US regulators to conduct investigations or bring or enforce actions against the company and non-us persons. NASDAQ says that creates concerns about the accuracy of disclosures, accountability, and access to information. Similarly, many corporate law experts agree that investors in issuers incorporated in the Cayman Islands have far less meaningful protections that investors and issuers domiciled in the United States. The Cayman Islands has erected a range of procedural barriers as part of their corporate law that precludes shareholders from holding directors and officers accountable, even when those directors and officers actively participate in corporate law breaking. As SEC Chair Paul Atkins indicated in his September 10th speech in Paris, foreign private issuers headquartered in China or incorporated in the Cayman Islands subject US investors to regulatory disclosure and governance frameworks that implicate shareholder interests. As a footnote to that comment, I would just highlight that the negative implications for shareholder interest derived from those frameworks are further exacerbated by the complex and opaque variable interest entity structures adopted by many foreign private issuers headquartered in China and incorporated in the Cayman Islands. The negative implications to investors of those variable interest entity structures are discussed in detail in CI Staffs recently issued report entitled Behind the Veil Risks of Chinese Companies and the BIE Structure freely available from CI's website www.cii.org. Just got to throw it in that commercial. A relevant question raised by the SEC's concept release is how the Commission might change the foreign private issuer regime to re establish that animating principle that Commissioner Purse talked about that foreign private issuer eligibility is appropriate for only for those companies that are subject to meaningful regulation disclosure obligations in their home country. You know, thinking about possible solutions to that question, and I acknowledge I didn't include a specific solution in the CII letter. I want to commend my Co panelist Paul Dudek for Co authoring one potential solution that I believe is worthy of the Commission's further consideration. That potential solution is described in pages 6 through 8 of the September 8th comment letter submitted by the Federal Regulation of Securities Committee of the Business Law Section, American Bar Association. As Paul can describe in more detail, I'll call it the ABA. Paul proposed alternative includes 3 key features and again he can discuss in a more detail, but one retains the current definition of foreign private issuer creates a new definition that addresses a subset of foreign private issuers that are not subject to meaningful regulation disclosure obligations in their home country. It does that by capturing in the new definition those foreign private issuers that have been identified by the Commission staff is having their equity securities traded almost exclusively in the US capital markets. And when you look at the SEC staff data contained in the concept release on that subset of foreign issuers, that would include more than 80% of the foreign private issuers with headquarters in China and more than 80% of the foreign private issuers incorporated in the Cayman Islands. So under my ABA Paul proposed solution, those foreign private issuers that fall under this new definition would be required to provide three additional regulatory disclosures that I believe at least with some minor improvements, many investors would find decision useful. First, the proposed additional disclosures would require that subset of foreign private issuers to file financial statements on a new Form 7K provided in a in a manner comparable to the information contained in Form 10 QS by domestic issuers, including a requirement that those foreign private issuers use the SEC's definition of materiality rather than some local definition. title: Let’s Talk Small Business with Molly Otter
description:
Learn about revenue financing as another way small businesses raise capital.  Molly Otter of Sage Growth Capital sits down with our SEC’s Small Business Advocacy team to talk about revenue financing, the challenges of non-coastal funding, the importance of networking, and her own insights running a small business.

*** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

Follow the SEC:
Twitter: https://twitter.com/SECGov
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/SECGov
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/us-securities-and-exchange-commission
transcript: Hi, my name is Kat Steinberg and I'm with the SEC Small Business Advocacy Team. Welcome to Let's Talk Small Business. In this episode I will be speaking with Molly Otter, who is co-founder and investment partner of Sage Grove Capital, an Idaho based investment fund focused on investing in early-stage businesses in Idaho and the Pacific Northwest using revenue-based financing. Before we get started, I want to note that everything I say today is on my own behalf, from my position in the office of the advocate for Small Business Capital formation and does not necessarily reflect the views of the Commission, any of the commissioners or any of my colleagues on the staff. Molly, it's great to see you and thank you for joining me. Thanks for having me, Kat. I'm excited to be here. Awesome. To kick us off. Would you please introduce yourself and tell our viewers a bit about your professional path? Sure. As you mentioned, I'm the co-founder and the investment partner for a company called Sage Growth Capital. We're based in Boise, Idaho, and we do revenue-based financing. Prior to that, I was the CIO, or the chief investment officer, for a company called Lighter Capital, which does SaaS based revenue-based financing across the country and is kind of considered the leading provider of that. And then before that, I was on Wall Street at a firm called AEA Investors. I did mezzanine and senior debt financing. So, I’ve spent my life on the debt side of the world and really enjoy it. As you mentioned, Sage Grove Capital focuses on revenue financing or what we sometimes hear called revenue-based financing. Can you give us a brief introduction to what it is, how it differs from traditional funding options like bank loans or equity, and how it fits into the small business capital formation ecosystem. Sure. So, revenue-based financing or revenue financing kind of sits between equity and debt. We like to say it has some of the good qualities of both. So, the way that Sage does it, we use a convertible note. So, like an equity or angel investment, that's the type of vehicle that we're using to make these investments. Unlike equity we don't take any equity ownership. So, it's a non-dilutive product. Like debt we get paid on a monthly basis. But unlike debt we don't get paid the same amount on a monthly basis. We get paid as a percentage of the company's revenue. So, when the company has a big month, they pay us more. When they have a smaller month, they pay us a lot less. And so we think it really helps align well with the company's revenues as they go over time. So might work really well for an education company that gets paid twice a year, or a SaaS business that has big annual contracts, that just gets paid once a year by its customers so that it spread, doesn't spread those payments equally over the year. Rather, those payments are made when you actually have the cash on hand and keep your gross margins consistent, from a cash accounting perspective. What's a typical range in size of an investment that your funds make? So our funds make investments from about $100,000 up to a million, but on average we're at about $250,000. And generally, we do multiple investments with the same company. So, we'll start out smaller and then add to those investments over a period of time. We like to align ourselves with the company's growth because as you can imagine, with revenue-based financing, as the company grows, the more we get, the faster we get paid back. So we want them to use our investments to grow their business, which also helps with the company. If they're using our investments wisely and their businesses are growing, then we can give them more capital at a less expensive cost. So it kind of works well for both parties. And so we tend to do smaller investments and then add on as the companies grow over time. And how large are the funds that you raise? So we raise a max of $10 million funds. We try to raise them every 2 to 3 years. So based on our investment thesis and how quickly we're putting money to work. But that's because on average, we're doing that $250,000 transactions. And so that's about 20 companies per fund, which is a lot of companies to manage from a portfolio perspective. But it works really well in the small business community, because about $250,000 seems to be a good area to start with, and not a lot of people write those size checks. And what is your investor’s average check side size? On our end, our investors are mostly angels, which is great. They send us a lot of their deal flow for companies that are going to be kind of the next, IPO or is there because we don't need that for our investments to work. And they are between 50 and $100,000. So we have a lot of investors in our funds, which is nice. I'd like to drill down on one of the characteristics of this type of financing and that is the non-dilutive funding. One of the recommendations regarding early-stage capital raising at this year's annual Small Business Forum was, “expand regional, federal and state options available for non-dilutive funding or debt forgiveness to support the earliest stages of entrepreneurship.” Molly, if Congress or the Commission were able to do that, what should that look like? Is that something where revenue financing could play a role? I definitely think revenue-based financing could play a role there because it is non-dilutive financing by its very nature. I don't think there are a lot of players out there who are doing it, who are taking capital or any equity. Sometimes there's warrants involved, but that's kind of limited. It is a great form of financing for businesses in terms of not taking that equity portion of it. I like there are probably other options out there that you could do. The problem with debt forgiveness is there is an IRS impact to the companies if you forgive debt. So that’s something that those companies have to think about longer term. Whereas with revenue based you're paying it down, so you're not going to have that debt forgiveness impact. I don't know enough about what other options there would be. I will say that one of the problems we run into as a small business ourselves is that each state has different regulations. And since we're not a national bank, but yet we have some bank like criteria to our investment, we have to be really careful about which states we go into and what the regulatory environment in each state is. So we go and look every time a new company comes to us in one of our contiguous states, that we may not have invested in, we have to go spend the legal resources to figure out if that state works, if we're going to run into any issues, if there's anything we need to be aware of, and that's getting more and more complicated in today's environment where, where you're headquartered and where you're incorporated may not be where people are actually sitting. So those type of things play a big role in our decision making. So if there were something on the national level that could make it easier to make these investments across the board without having to do individual state analysis, I think that that would be really helpful. Agreed. Agreed. Switching gears, you are in a non-coastal area, so we hear from entrepreneurs and others often that if you aren't situated in one of the coasts or in a major hub, securing funding for your small business can be more difficult. You're located in Boise, Idaho, and you focus your investments in non-coastal regions. What are some of the challenges you see that are unique to or heightened for funds and entrepreneurs outside traditional hubs? Well, there's definitely less capital providers sitting in places like Boise Idaho. We are very unique in our region. There are there has been some uptick of people doing financing in Boise, but when we started, we were kind of the only people in the game. And I think that's interesting. I also think that there are great benefits to being in small areas. Like when we started, the governor's office was excited that we were starting a business here. Like, that's not something you're going to get in New York State. So you kind of have to take the good with the bad. And as a small business, you have to think, okay, what are the things that I can use to my advantage? It’s a small community, so I bet if I meet one person, they're going to know five other people in my community that may know who the right funding source for me is. And so that may actually be easier if you're willing to get out and go to a couple different meetings and do coffees with people to get to know them, because with a small with these non-coastal areas, people all know each other. So, they're more likely to be able to make the right introduction for you faster than maybe on the coasts you would see. So I think we have to kind of take the good with the bad on that and, go with it. I mean, you know, there are less capital sources for sure, but that doesn't mean people aren't putting money to work and are interested in investing in good companies. That brings me to something else we've been told repeatedly, and that is that networking and building your community is one of the most important things a founder can do while growing their company and seeking capital. What practical advice would you offer an entrepreneur who thinks they want to bring on investors, or even just wants to start building their network? Yeah, I mean, it is the most important thing is getting out there and meeting people. And I would say go to your, you know, local chamber of commerce, get to know the people who are out there. In Boise, we have something called Trailhead, which is the local-run organization that tries to help companies start up, small businesses start up. So there are lots of organizations like that. And you do kind of really have to go out there and meet people. As I was mentioning before, most of the investors in Sage are angels. And because of that, they're out there having a lot of coffees, and we get 90% of our deal flow through them saying, hey, I met this person. It wasn't the right fit for my style of investing, but it might be the right fit for Sage and making those introductions. So it's really about just going out and meeting people. And I know that that's sometimes hard as a founder because you're like, I have to focus on building the business I'm trying to build. But a lot of your time really does have to be spent out there introducing yourself to the community. Because if the community doesn't know who you are, they're not going to be able to point you in the right direction in terms of finding the investors that work for you. Great advice. If you've watched our previous Let's Talk Small Business episodes, you know that we like to end on a light note with a lightning round. A quick question for a quick answer. If you were to start a small business, what would it be, Molly? Well, I think sage is a small business, but on top of that, I would start a bag's business for going to camp with kids. I have three kids who go to camp, and it is always a disaster they could never find at say that they can't find the stuff that I have packed for them, or come back missing half of it, or it's just totally disorganized. And as a Type-A personality that drives me a little bananas. So I would, I have looked into this with another mom who is in the same boat, and we were like, we need to do a better bag for camp, because the trunks are too big and the bags are too light and it just doesn't work. So that would be what I would do. As a fellow mom. I look forward to seeing that on the market. Good luck. Thank you. Molly, this was fun. Thank you for joining me today. I am excited for more entrepreneurs to learn about revenue-based financing as another way to fund their small businesses. Well, thank you so much for the time, Kat. I really appreciate it. Absolutely. Hope to see you soon. Thanks. Bye.

I look forward to the thoughtful panel discussion ahead and the discussion concerning a recommendation. Now we will turn to opening remarks, first from Chairman Atkins and then the other Commissioners. Chairman Atkins. Well, thank you very much, Brian and good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Having just returned myself from the UK and Europe, I had a chance to address this very topic and I can say how timely today's panel is. It's also very timely and fitting for the FCA to be represented here today in light of a long collaboration of our two countries in the financial markets. Both of our countries have vibrant capital markets, and I look forward to working with our UK counterparts to enhance our mutual cooperation and harmonization of regulatory approaches to promote innovation and economic growth. As I stated last week in London and before the OECD in Paris, strong sovereign nations like the United States must continue to engage constructively in the world in ways that promote our prosperity. And at the SEC, these priorities find expression in our work to attract foreign companies to the US markets and to provide Americans with the opportunity to invest in those companies while ensuring that US and foreign firms experience a level playing field. In the early 1980's, the SEC developed the foundations of its current standard for which foreign companies qualify for special accommodations. These accommodations recognize the differences in business and market practices, accounting standards, and corporate governance requirements, among other matters, between the US and foreign companies. Over the decade, the SEC has reassessed and reformed its standard as needed to address changes in the global markets and to protect US investors. And one of my first actions as Chairman, I asked the Commission to approve the issuance of a concept release to gather public feedback on whether the standards should be updated to reflect the evolution in financial markets and corporate legal structures. This concept release solicits broad public feedback on whether foreign companies listed in the United States should be subject to additional conditions, such as a minimum foreign trading volume or listing on a major foreign exchange for them to receive accommodations not available to U.S. companies. Now, to be clear, the SEC welcomes foreign companies that seek to access the US capital markets. And we start by listening to experienced expert market participants. We will begin today with remarks from SEC Chairman Atkins, Acting CFTC Chairman Pham and SEC Commissioner Crenshaw will follow. Our first panel will lay the groundwork of historical context for our discussion today. Our second panel will provide perspective from trading platforms, followed by remarks from SEC Commissioner Uyeda. Well, thank you very much, Jamie, and good afternoon, and thank everyone here for joining us either in person or, of course, you know, online. I should also like to thank Acting Chairman Pham, as well as SEC and CFTC staff for organizing this joint roundtable with a little advance notice and of course, our stellar group of panelists for lending their time and expertise. Today's program today, I believe, marks a turning point in the history of American financial markets. For too long, the SEC and the CFTC have operated in parallel lanes, too often in conflict with each other, leaving the American public to bear the cost of duplication, delay and uncertainty. That era is behind us. We are charting a new course, one that will solidify America's position as the world's financial leader today. I look forward to hearing from industry leaders on how the two agencies can better coordinate on behalf of the American public. *** About The Securities and Exchange Commission ***

The mission of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. The SEC strives to promote a market environment that is worthy of the public's trust.

So our panel is going to focus on the role of the trade through prohibition in today's market structure. We're going to touch on a variety of the issues and number of them are going to be similar to the topics that were discussed this morning. We're going to talk about the intersection of, of, of trade through prohibitions and the duty of best execution, of course.
